newsitem.title: USA: Misled Prudential policyholders should choose ADR.
newsitem.headline: Misled Prudential policyholders should choose ADR.

text.p: Prudential Insurance Co of America policyholders who believe they were misled by the company's sales agents should choose the alternative dispute resolution (ADR) process offered in the company's proposed settlement.

"If you were misled, there's no argument not to do the ADR," said Brad Friedman, a partner with firm Milberg, Weiss, Bershad Hynes & Lerach, which is representing policyholders in the class-action against Prudential.
Even if policyholders have no written evidence to prove the deception, they still have a good chance of receiving some compensation under the ADR process, he said.
"Everyone who was misled should do it," he said in a telephone interview with Reuters. "Everyone."

Policyholders who purchased permanent life insurance between 1982 and 1995 began receiving notices in February about the opportunity to receive remediation if they were harmed by improper sales practices.
The notification includes a yellow election form, asking policyholders to choose between the ADR process and basic claim relief.
Policyholders must return the election form by June 1.
The ADR process and basic claim relief are essential elements of Prudential's proposed class-action settlement of deceptive sales practice complaints.
The settlement must win the approval of a federal judge before taking effect. A decision is expected soon after March 3.
The ADR process offers policyholders, at no cost, the potential for at least a partial refund plus interest.
The basic claim relief, however, simply offers enhanced life insurance, annuities and low-cost premium loans to policyholders who purchased permanent life insurance from 1982 to 1995.
The basic claim relief, Friedman said, should be selected by policyholders who do not believe they were misled.

"If you don't feel you were misled, nobody made any kind of a vanishing premium promise to you, nobody churned your policy...basically nobody lied to you when they sold you the policy, then you should take basic claim relief," he said.
Policyholders who choose to participate in the ADR process will receive a claim form in the mail, asking them to tell their story, Friedman said.
Policyholders also will be asked to respond to several questions and to submit copies of any documents that support their story, he said.
If there is no written evidence, he said, policyholders should write down the oral or verbal misrepresentations and whether there were any witnesses to it, he said.
The claim then will be evaluated and scored to determine how much relief policyholders should receive.
"If you have drop dead terrific evidence you may do better than if you don't," he said.
"However, even if you are relying solely upon your sworn word, because these are under penalty of perjury, that counts for something," he said.
Policyholders will qualify for a full refund plus interest if their claim scores a three and will qualify for at least a partial refund if their claim scores a two.
With a score of one, a policyholder will be eligible for basic claim relief.
Policyholders will receive nothing only if their claim scores a zero and to do that there must be no evidence to support the claim and, instead, evidence that they are lying, Friedman said.
"To get a zero, you really have to deserve it," he said.

Claims will get a score of three on the basis of any one of the following: if the policyholder's or company's documents confirm the claim, if the agent confirms the claim, or if the agent committed forgery by executing the policyholder's signature without authority.
Claims will also get a score of three if material company documents were improperly destroyed or if the agent was fired, disciplined or fined for improper sales practices.
A score of two will be awarded if the misstatements are not in writing and the agent denies the misstatements, and on balance, the available evidence supports the claim.
A policyholder's word "means a tremendous amount," Friedman said. "All sorts of people will get twos and threes with nothing more than their word."
Claims also will receive a score of two, if there are at least three complaints against the agent or there is a pattern of inappropriate activity.

Claims will get a score of one if there is no complaint history against the agent, the misstatements are not in writing and are denied by the agent, and the available evidence neither supports nor undermines the claim.
If a claim does not win a score of three on the first evaluation, it will automatically be reviewed by another independent claim team.
Policyholders may then appeal the decision if they are not satisfied.
"If you really have no reason to complain and you're not upset about anything and nothing untoward happened to you, you should not take advantage of ADR," Friedman said.
"But anyone who feels anything bad did happen to them should take ADR and should not be dissuaded from possibly getting a zero," he said.
"Because if you think something bad happened to you, the chances of there being affirmative evidence that you're lying about it is remote at best," he said.
